prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Code · Config options with long tokens (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Option" · longest unbreakable word 131px · one-line width 131px
  col 2: header "Default" · longest unbreakable word 90px · one-line width 334px
  col 3: header "Example" · longest unbreakable word 537px · one-line width 537px
  col 4: header "Description" · longest unbreakable word 83px · one-line width 501px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 720px. You MAY choose a total wider than 719px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

These are all candidate designs you produced, rendered in a real browser:
Design r1A: widths [152, 140, 230, 197] · table 720×474px · row heights [36, 60, 83, 106, 106, 83] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 3
Design r1B: widths [152, 111, 290, 166] · table 720×474px · row heights [36, 60, 83, 106, 106, 83] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 1
Design r1C: widths [152, 165, 558, 200] · table 1076×428px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 106, 106, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 356px
Design r2A: widths [152, 111, 558, 200] · table 1022×428px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 106, 106, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 302px
Design r2B: widths [152, 111, 558, 166] · table 988×474px · row heights [36, 60, 83, 106, 106, 83] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 268px
Design r3A: widths [152, 145, 290, 132] · table 720×567px · row heights [36, 83, 106, 106, 153, 83] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 6 lines · mid-word splits 1
Design r3B: widths [152, 120, 310, 137] · table 720×544px · row heights [36, 83, 106, 106, 129, 83] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 5 lines · mid-word splits 1
Design r3C: widths [152, 120, 280, 167] · table 720×474px · row heights [36, 60, 83, 106, 106, 83] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 2

Decide as a designer:
- "preferred": the best design(s). Name more than one only if they are genuinely equally good.
- "acceptable": other designs a careful designer would still publish.
- "bad": designs with clear visual faults, each with the fault. If none of these is clearly bad, also return ONE deliberately bad but plausible alternative as "contrast" widths and say what is wrong with it.
- "ranges": for each column, the px range within which the preferred design stays equally good (keep other columns' proportions).
- "rationale": 2–4 concrete sentences about this table.
- "principles": observations that seem GENERAL (likely to hold for other tables) vs SPECIFIC to this case.
- "tradeoffs" and "uncertain": what reasonable designers could disagree on.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"preferred":["name"],"acceptable":["name"],"bad":[{"design":"name","why":""}],"contrast":{"widths":[int px],"why":""} or null,"ranges":[[min,max]],"rationale":"","principles":{"general":[""],"specific":[""]},"tradeoffs":"","uncertain":""}

The overflow designs buy fewer splits by forcing horizontal scrolling and hiding Description, which is worse for row-by-row comparison. r3B is a credible fallback, but it spends width on Default and starves Description, making the table taller.","principles":{"general":["Set a column's floor from its longest unbreakable token plus padding; code/URL columns should not go below that unless horizontal scrolling is acceptable.","Give the column with long machine-readable values the dominant width; short scalar columns can be narrow.","For a compact reference table, prefer one benign break over horizontal scrolling, but avoid multiple mid-token breaks in identifiers and URLs.","Narrowing Description raises every row's height; total width fitting is not enough if the table becomes a tall ribbon."],"specific":["Option needs about 152px because 'cache.ttlSeconds' is 131px; it cannot shrink without splitting.","Example needs roughly 290px to keep the PostgreSQL and JWKS URLs at two lines; 230px produces three ugly splits.","Default can be 111px because most values are short; only the log pattern wraps to four lines.","Description at 166px wraps to four lines; at 132px it dominates row height and makes the table 567px tall."]},"tradeoffs":"A designer could accept horizontal scrolling to keep every token unbroken (r1C/r2A/r2B), or accept a taller table with a narrower Description (r3A/r3B). The chosen compromise prioritizes no horizontal scroll and compact rows over eliminating every break.","uncertain":"Whether a single hyphen break in 'well-known' is acceptable in a code table; whether r3C's smaller height is worth its extra mid-word split; and whether r3B's 544px height is preferable to r1B's tighter 474px."}
